Three genuine issues remain:

1. **`splitChild(childIndex, children[childIndex])` — the `child` parameter is always derivable from `childIndex`**, making it redundant at every call site.
2. **`collectKeys` checks `if (!leaf)` on every loop iteration** — `leaf` is fixed for the node's lifetime, so the check belongs outside the loop.
3. **`containsKey` ends with two statements that collapse to one** — `if (leaf) return false; return children[i].containsKey(key)` is just `return !leaf && children[i].containsKey(key)`.

content.text:
**`splitChild(childIndex)` drops the redundant `child` parameter.** Every call site was `splitChild(idx, children[idx])` — the child was always `children[childIndex]`, never anything else. Passing it separately was redundant ceremony. The method now resolves `child` from `children[childIndex]` on its first line, where it reads as a clear local introduction rather than a caller obligation.

**`collectKeys` hoists the leaf check out of the loop.** `leaf` is `final` and set at construction — it never changes. Checking `!leaf` on every iteration was a repeated test of a fixed condition. Splitting into two branches makes each path a clean, unconditional loop, and the internal-node path no longer needs to interleave the child descent with the check.

**`containsKey` tail collapses to one expression.** `if (leaf) return false; return children[i].containsKey(key)` is two statements expressing one thing: recurse into children only if not a leaf. `return !leaf && children[i].containsKey(key)` says exactly that, with short-circuit evaluation doing the leaf guard.
